Solution 1 never reaches a final answer. Its output is truncated mid-computation and ends at "79". Its recurrence is also wrong: when exactly one of Michael or James is selected and wins, both remain in the game and can still meet later, so that case does not contribute 0.

Solution 2 reaches 1/2 by invoking a "2/g" heuristic without justification. The exact recurrence below shows this is not the answer for n = 34.

Solution 3 sets up the correct recurrence. Let P(n) be the probability that the two meet when n players remain. Both are selected with probability 12/(n(n−1)). Exactly one is selected and wins with probability 2(n−4)/(n(n−1)). Neither is selected with probability (n−4)(n−5)/(n(n−1)). Summing the last two cases gives

P(n) = 12/(n(n−1)) + [(n−4)(n−3)/(n(n−1))] · P(n−3).

With P(4) = 1, the formula P(n) = 4/n satisfies this recurrence: substituting P(n−3) = 4/(n−3) gives (12 + 4(n−4))/(n(n−1)) = 4/n. It also matches a direct check for n = 7, where P(7) = 4/7. Therefore P(34) = 4/34 = 2/17. Solution 3's reasoning is sound and its answer is correct.

VERDICT 1: REJECT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: ACCEPT
